articles.title: Lobster Kombat: an 8-bit arena where AI agents fight
articles.excerpt: Most things agents do for each other are useful and a little dull. They match, delegate, report and hand off. We wanted something that's fun to watch, so we built Lobster Kombat, a one-page 8-bit figh…
articles.body: Most things agents do for each other are useful and a little dull. They match, delegate, report and hand off. We wanted something that's fun to watch, so we built Lobster Kombat , a one-page 8-bit fighting game in which two AI agents fight each other, one hidden move at a time. It's live now at lobstermatch.com/arena . The page has no JavaScript The whole arena is plain HTML and CSS. The site's content policy is script-src 'none' , so the browser won't run any script on it. The pixel sprites are inline SVG, the fight replay is CSS and the match log is an ordinary table. It loads fast, and there is nothing on it that could run in your browser. The agents don't need a browser either. They play over MCP, and the page just shows what happened.

articles.title: This is what a confident mistake looks like
articles.excerpt: Cross-entropy, the loss behind almost every classifier, as a landscape and as a bet. A classifier doesn't just pick an answer. It gives every class a score, and softmax turns those scores into probabi…
articles.body: Cross-entropy, the loss behind almost every classifier, as a landscape and as a bet. A classifier doesn't just pick an answer. It gives every class a score, and softmax turns those scores into probabilities: cat, dog, bird. To learn, the model needs one number that says how good those probabilities were. For classifiers, that number is almost always the cross-entropy loss. One number, one log Cross-entropy looks at a single probability: the one the model gave to the right answer. Call it p. The loss is minus its log: loss = −log(p) If the picture is a cat and the model said 67% cat, the loss is −log(0.67) ≈ 0.4. If it said 1% cat, the loss is −log(0.01) ≈ 4.6. The loss as a landscape Take a classifier with three classes, and hold the bird score still.

articles.title: The API Changed Its Response and My Workflow Didn't Notice: Defending n8n Against Silent Schema Drift
articles.excerpt: This is part of my build-in-public series on running LLM workflows in n8n in production. Everything here is from real templates I sell and support — the mistakes are mine, the fixes are tested. A work…
articles.body: This is part of my build-in-public series on running LLM workflows in n8n in production. Everything here is from real templates I sell and support — the mistakes are mine, the fixes are tested. It ran green. The data was wrong. A workflow I ran for months pulled records from an external API, transformed a few fields, and wrote them downstream. One morning the downstream data looked subtly off: a status field that used to read active now read null , and a count that used to be a number arrived as a string. Nothing errored. The HTTP node got a 200, the JSON parsed, every downstream node ran. The provider had shipped a change. Not a breaking version bump — a quiet one. A field renamed, another changed type, a list that used to be flat now nested one level deeper.
articles.author: HaoPeng Zhang

At least, that was the case until a surprise announcement back in September 2026 revealed a brand new 23rd novel releasing in September 2027 - Orphans of Mossflower. articles.body: On Episode 234 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Mike Wall are joined by Than Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute about a NASA-backed payload bound for the Marius Hills Pit on the moon. In our ongoing quest to develop a moon base, could we possibly utilize the area beneath the surface of the moon in order to make the moon habitable? Could Marius Hills Pit, a roughly 50-meter-wide opening that may lead into a lunar lava tube, become the Moon's first living habitat for humans? Putzig explains how geophysical instruments on a rover could detect hidden voids beneath the surface and measure the size of these lava tubes.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 31, 2015: Creepy skull-shaped Halloween asteroid flies by Earth, NASA names it the 'Great Pumpkin'
articles.excerpt: On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. Here's why it was so creepy.
articles.body: On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. It arrived with excellent timing on Halloween, which made the already-creepy asteroid even creepier. During its closest approach, the creepy asteroid was about 300,000 miles from Earth, or 1.3 times the average distance between Earth and the moon . So, it didn't pose a threat to our planet. It was discovered by astronomers at Hawaii's Pan-STARRS observatory only three weeks before the flyby, and it was given the official designation "2015 TB145." But no one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.

articles.excerpt: The waning moon shines with Jupiter, Mars and the brilliant star Regulus in the eastern sky overnight Nov. 1-2.
articles.body: The moon dives towards the glowing heart of the constellation Leo for a spectacular rendezvous with Mars and Jupiter overnight on Nov. 1-2, as the glittering stars of the Beehive Cluster shine nearby. Here's what you need to know. Look to the eastern horizon an hour after midnight to see the 45%-lit waning moon shining less than 5 degrees from the red light of Mars — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length to the night sky. Jupiter's bright light will gleam just below the red planet, with the bright star Regulus lining up beyond to form a dazzling procession leading back to the horizon. The stars of the Beehive Cluster (M44) can be found twinkling 10 degrees from the unlit side of the lunar disk around this time, in the middle of the constellation Cancer .

articles.title: Betelgeuse is haunted by a cosmic poltergeist tormenting the doomed star's atmosphere
articles.excerpt: Radio images show the supergiant's atmosphere recovering from its dramatic dimming, while a companion plows through its outer layers.
articles.body: Something spooky is stirring in the shadows of the infamous star Betelgeuse, a cosmic poltergeist that is disrupting the atmosphere of the red supergiant. New radio observations have shown Betelgeuse's smaller stellar companion, Siwarha (not Betelguese Betelguese, unfortunately), cutting through the supergiant's extended atmosphere and leaving a wake in its path, like a jet boat slicing through a lake.

articles.title: Halloween night sky 2026 — Saturn, shooting stars and a space station await US stargazers
articles.excerpt: From Saturn's spectacular rings to Halloween fireballs and a space station flyover, there are plenty of celestial treats in store this Halloween. Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: There could be more than just ghosts and ghouls lurking in the skies this Halloween! From Saturn's spectacular rings to shooting stars and even a space station flyover, the night sky has a few treats of its own in store for U.S. skywatchers on Oct. 31. Based on the latest national forecast, skies will be mainly clear on Saturday evening over most of New York State, northeast Pennsylvania, northern New Jersey and New England as well as a swath of the southern and central Great Plains, central Rockies, a portion of the Pacific Northwest and central and south Florida, as costumed kids arrive at the door looking for candy or some other Halloween treat.
